‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation


Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive




The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.
In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.

Delgado’s milk production has fallen by half. As the dry season approaches, he is selling off cattle for fear of what is to come. He says: “I and other producers have had to slaughter or sell animals of high genetic value simply to avoid the heartbreaking prospect of watching them die of thirst or starvation. The lack of water has greatly affected us, and it is going to continue to do so.”
Panama is gripped by a water crisis. A rainy season punctuated by drought, exacerbated by the climate crisis, has ravaged large swathes of the country. El Niño threatens to continue the havoc. In August, the government declared a national state of emergency that will remain in place until June 2027. Authorities forecast rainfall deficits of more than 50% in some regions until December.


View image in fullscreen
A farmer crosses the Indio River on his horse at Tres Hermanas community, one of the towns threatened by the reservoir project. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters
“The situation is dramatic,” says Panama’s environment minister, Juan Navarro. “Climate change has undoubtedly increased the frequency and also the gravity of El Niño, as well as other climate extremes; we used to get an El Niño every 10 or 20 years. The last, in 2023, cost the Panama canal almost a billion dollars in revenue.”







How the climate crisis threatens the Panama Canal – and the country’s future

And this latest El Niño, Navarro says, citing scientists, is pointing towards being the worst in history. He says: “We are already starting to feel the impact, but we have seen nothing yet. For Panama, this is life or death. The canal is life and death for our economy, and for our drinking water supply.”

Do not be distracted by other global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now

Steven Guilbeault


In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action





When I was five, property developers came to cut down the woods behind my home in La Tuque, Quebec. My mother encouraged me to climb one of the trees in protest, then told the developers, straight-faced, that there was nothing she could do when they asked her to get me down. A few days later, the tree was cut down anyway.
I thought about that tree in the early hours of a freezing Montreal morning in December 2022, as the gavel came down on a global agreement between nearly 200 countries to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. I thought about how important nature is for our health, our food security and our economies, but also how much passion there is around protecting it, and how it has the power to inspire people all around the world.

Despite differences in national circumstances, interests, and levels of responsibility, what we agreed to do really did, and still does, have the power to create longer term stability for billions of people across borders. We agreed to protect 30% of the world’s land and oceans and channel $200bn (£150bn) a year into nature. We admitted that far more money was flowing into destroying nature than protecting it, committing to address $500bn of subsidies currently contributing to the problem.


View image in fullscreen
Steven Guilbeault speaks to journalists after Cop15 in Montreal in 2022.  Photograph: Lars Hagberg/AFP/Getty Images
Nearly four years later, the reality is that we are not delivering on those promises.
The context has changed. War, extreme weather and homes swept away or burned to the ground are becoming the norm, and public finances are strained everywhere. Leaders feel pressure to choose between protecting biodiversity, which is perceived as a “nice-to-have”, and policies that look like self-preservation.
This is a false dichotomy. Nature is a critical asset for national prosperity and economic security, and the evidence is already there.
Farmers in France who have leant on biodiversity instead of chemical fertilisers have seen crops thrive through extreme drought. In Brazil, Indigenous fire brigades have cut blazes by more than 20% in parts of the Cerrado and Amazon, regions vital to the soya and commodity trade with the global north.

He said Northern Ireland was a small nation that could be "agile and innovative" in tackling challenges like increasing renewable energy, improving waste management and reducing emissions.
But he warned that a failure to act would mean missing out on innovation opportunities, paying more for energy and damaging the health of children.
The committee is an independent body advising the UK and devolved governments on emissions targets.
Over the course of a two-day visit, Topping is meeting farmers, people from the business sector and politicians.

articles.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world
articles.raw_rss: As the strongest El Niño on record continues to intensify, what impacts on weather patterns are already being felt across the globe? Sarah Keith-Lucas looks at the evidence.
articles.raw_meta: As the strongest El Niño on record continues to intensify, what impacts on weather patterns are already being felt across the globe? Sarah Keith-Lucas looks at the evidence.
articles.jina_text:
El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.
Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.
The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.
Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world.





Image caption, 

Several regions around the world are already experiencing anticipated El Niño impacts



Indonesia battles worst wildfire season since 2015




Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El Niño years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015.
This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned. 
This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El Niño.
The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness.
More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.



East Pacific explodes with hurricane activity




In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far. 
There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes. 
This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.
Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.
Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.
The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño.
Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo. 
Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month. 
Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie. 
Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.








Atlantic hurricane season remains eerily quiet




In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.
El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.
There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.

A life-sized statue of Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, was unveiled and promptly began melting in front of an audience in Tallahassee in a symbolic protest at his rejection of action on the climate crisis.
The silvery statue, revealed to an audience of onlookers last week, melted away to show a skull under DeSantis’s face. The structure was cast from solid gallium, a metal that melts at 85.6F (29.8C), which is below summertime high temperatures frequently reached in Tallahassee, Florida’s capital.

‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline


As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps 




Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, a study has found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.
Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.

The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed.



Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress.
Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”.
“The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added.
The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known as Cop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources.

Full SummaryHonduran farmer Milexi Rodríguez describes how access to water infrastructure, loans and training helped her rebuild after the 2023 El Niño drought and how similar support could enable other women farmers in Honduras to withstand future extreme weather.
Like every farmer in Honduras, I do not need models or forecasts to tell me what impact a powerful El Niño can have.
I have lived this before. In my small hometown of Olanchito alone, the extreme El Niño of 2023 brought a drought that killed more than a thousand cattle, mine among them. After years of working towards my own land, starting with just one cow, I had to start again from scratch.
Raising cattle as a woman already comes with its own challenges, from the physical demands of the work to the prejudices that we face. Losing an entire herd to drought despite all of my efforts was devastating. But it was also a valuable lesson in how to be more resilient.





The same conditions that took my cattle in 2023 are back. Drought alerts are in place for 233 out of 298 municipalities, including red alerts for more than 100. A severe lack of rain is destroying crops and leaving livestock without enough food and water.
The difference for me, at least, is that I’ve been able to rebuild stronger since 2023.

Britain's woodlands are facing an unlikely threat. One of our most recognisable and admired wild animals, are putting increasing pressure on the landscapes they inhabit. With few natural predators to keep their numbers in check, the growing deer population are browsing young trees, stripping away vegetation and preventing woodland from regenerating naturally. The consequences extend far beyond the trees themselves, affecting the plants, insects, birds and other wildlife that depend on healthy, diverse habitats.
We have become accustomed to thinking that protecting nature means leaving it untouched, yet in a landscape altered by human activity, sometimes intervention is essential. Carefully managed deer populations can give woodlands the opportunity to recover, allowing new growth and creating the conditions for biodiversity to flourish.
But what happens to the animals removed as part of that management? While venison can enter the food chain, their skins have often been treated as waste. Now, a British tannery and a Norfolk design studio are demonstrating how a material that might otherwise be discarded can become something valuable, beautiful and enduring.





Their collaboration raises a provocative question: what if taking something from nature could, under the right circumstances, be part of protecting it?

Jack Millington, founder of Billy Tannery, understands the relationship between agriculture, materials and design better than most. Growing up on a dairy farm in the Midlands, his father ran the farm, his mother a successful interior designer, he was surrounded by two seemingly contradictory worlds.

As such, they effectively bring down the cost of a heat pump to roughly the same level as a standard gas combi boiler – which average around £3,800 for a typical three-bedroom home.



 
Once a heat pump is installed, a typical household could save between £110 and £350 a year compared to using a conventional gas boiler, according to Nesta, the research and innovation charity. With energy bills predicted to jump by 16 per cent to £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household in January, these kinds of savings are more important than ever. 
Heat pumps typically take heat from the air outside the home (and less often the ground), bring it inside and warm it to the required temperature. But because most of the heat is transferred from the surroundings rather than generated from scratch, they are three to five times more efficient than gas central heating. 
And because they run on electricity, they are much better for the environment than gas-burning boilers – especially if it’s generated from low-carbon sources such as wind, solar and nuclear power, which now provide the majority of the UK’s electricity. 
This gives heat pumps the added benefit of improving your energy efficiency, or EPC, rating. That’s rapidly becoming very important, with strict new minimum requirements of an EPC C rating due to be implemented on rented properties in 2030, something many of them don’t currently achieve.



 
To put the environmental performance of a heat pump into perspective, replacing an old G-rated boiler with a modern A-rated one would typically add three to 10 EPC points, according to the Home Energy Check website (with each of the seven EPC grades spanning an average of 14 points, but with more points per grade lower down the scale and fewer points higher up). 
By contrast, if you replace your G-rated boiler with a standard air-source heat pump, you can expect to jump from EPC band E or D to band C or even B – with the caveat that the property does need to be reasonably well insulated for that scale of benefit. 
But, however many plus points heat pumps have, any significant cut to the grants will inevitably put most people off buying one.

Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian town as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals


Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the fastest-warming places in the world




Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.
Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.







In the fastest-warming town on the planet you can’t drink the tap water. Here’s why – video
Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade.
Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining town.
“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.


View image in fullscreen
Marjolaine Verret takes water samples. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian
When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.”
The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”.
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.

The government must hold an inquiry into the unequal impacts of air pollution, 150 scientists, MPs and activists have urged.
Research by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that across England, lower-income areas have persistently higher levels of air pollution than wealthier areas.

The same research found that minority-ethnic populations were exposed to air pollution levels that were about 6% higher than those experienced by white populations.
In a letter coordinated by the charity Enact Equality and signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including the climate activist Greta Thunberg, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been urged to hold a national inquiry into the impacts of air pollution on these groups.
Exposure to air pollution is linked to heart disease, strokes, cancer, asthma and effects on lung development in children. Despite this, the letter says, the UK does not have a dedicated mechanism to address the health inequalities.







London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?

Read more
Air pollution can come from a wide range of sources, from wood-burning stoves to industrial fossil fuel burning. But the leading threat to clean air is posed by traffic emissions, with petrol and diesel vehicles emitting a variety of toxic pollutants. Measures such as London’s ultra-low emission zone have had a significant impact on improving air quality, with children’s lungs found to have grown bigger and stronger as a result of the policy.
While there has been marked progress in reducing air pollution in cities like London, new government data shows that in 2025, parts of London, Glasgow and Bristol still had illegal levels of air pollution.
Rosamund Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, the mother of a nine-year-old girl who became the first person in the UK to have air pollution cited on their death certificate, said a “failure of inaction by all the main political parties over so many years, has meant the UK population is exposed to illegal levels of emissions”.


This warning comes as new data, obtained through freedom of information requests by the campaign group Mums for Lungs, shows that in 11 English cities and areas, including London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham, more than 200,000 children were taken to hospital with breathing difficulties in 2025. The research found that younger children were the most affected, with more than 120,000 babies and toddlers admitted to A&E or hospital.
Children are particularly vulnerable to air pollution because their lungs are still developing and they breathe more air relative to their body size than adults.
In the city of Manchester, there has been a stark increase in admissions of babies and toddlers, rising from 653 in 2023 to 1,072 in 2025.

As efforts to protect people from extreme heat stall, organizers are embracing an approach that targets major brands’ reputations




“It’s the kind of heat that makes you feel like you’re being dehydrated, like your skin is drying out,” said Lucas Benitez, after harvesting watermelons with his sons and wife this summer. “The heat that we had 30 years ago is not nearly the heat that we have today.”
This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and most workers in fields, greenhouses and unconditioned indoor facilities still do not have heat protections on the job, putting their health at risk as the climate crisis is expected to make extreme heat more frequent and intense.

Benitez began working in tomato fields in Immokalee, Florida when he was just 16, and in the early 1990s went on to help found the Coalition of Immokalee Workers (CIW), named after the major tomato growing region in south-west Florida. Today, CIW’s fair food program has some of the strongest heat protections for workers in the country, and its approach is being emulated by other groups – in the US and beyond – as federal, state and local efforts to protect people from extreme heat stall.
The program’s protections were hard won after years of boycotts, hunger strikes and protests against food corporations. The model, described as “market-based enforcement” by academics, works by targeting the reputation of the known brand-name of a company – say a fast-food retailer – to improve conditions rather than smaller entities in the supply chain.


View image in fullscreen
Workers pick tomatoes at a farm owned and operated by Pacific Tomato Growers in Immokalee. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images
Retailers agree to pay a small premium to buy from farms that comply with a worker-protection code of conduct. Farms that violate the code can lose their preferred status, giving workers a powerful way to enforce protections without relying on government regulators.


Miami-based WeCount is among the labor groups that are now adopting the fair food program model for other hot, low-wage jobs. Worker organizations in dairy production in Vermont, construction in Minnesota, sugarcane production in India, and banana production in Ecuador have created similar human rights initiatives.
Florida produces about 70% of all indoor plants sold in the US. The workers who grow these plants were exposed to temperatures over 100F (37.8C) this summer and reported heat-related symptoms and dehydration, said Oscar Londoño, the co-executive director of WeCount, a human rights organization led by immigrant workers and families in south Florida.
“Workers feel like they’re on the verge of fainting,” Londoño said. “We have, unfortunately, far too many stories of heatstroke.”

While some personal loan providers may be able to offer interest rates close to zero per cent, the majority of larger lenders will offer loans in the region of 2-4%, according to multiple sources. 



 
The low interest loans will cover heat pumps, solar and batteries, but won’t cover insulation. It comes amid rumours that the Government is preparing to cut its Boiler Upgrade Scheme, which offers non-repayable grants for heat pumps.  
How will the new loan scheme work? 
The Government is funding lenders to help them provide green loans with lower interest rates than the deals currently on offer.  
There are currently a limited number of low interest rate loans for green upgrades on the market, but they usually have tight restrictions. For example Nationwide offers a zero per cent green upgrade loan for its mortgage customers for a duration of two or five years.   
Mainstream personal loans typically have higher interest rates, with the best rates sitting at around 5.9 per cent APR. 



 
Under the Government’s new scheme, the Treasury will pay participating lenders up to 20 per cent of the loan amount, which will allow lenders to offer deals with rates up to five percentage points lower than they otherwise would have. 
For example, if a lender currently offers solar panel loans with an interest rate of seven per cent then they could offer deals with an interest rate of two per cent by joining the Government’s scheme. 
The full list of lenders participating in the scheme is yet to be announced, but is expected to include a range of organisations, including high street banks and Buy Now Pay Later lenders.  
What can you fund using the loans? 
The loans will be for a minimum of three years and will cover the following technologies: 
 
Solar panels – up to £15,000 
Electrical storage battery – up to £15,000 
Air-water source heat pump – up to £20,000 
Air-air source heat pump – up to £10,000 
Ground source heat pump – up to £35,000  
Biomass boiler – up to £20,000  
Heat network connection – up to £7,500   
Micro-renewable system (such as domestic wind turbine) – up to £20,000  
What are the limitations? 
The loans will not cover insulation, which is often recommended for households installing heat pumps to help the heat pump work efficiently.  
James Dyson, Senior Researcher at the climate change think tank E3G said the loans will be “helpful” for people looking to “protect themselves from high gas prices”, but said it was “a shame they can’t be used to pay for insulation, which helps people to stay warm and keep their bills low”.

The Victorian election put gas laws on the ballot. The Coalition and One Nation have chosen to fight for the indefensible

Saul Griffith


The ‘right to choose’ crowd would damage Victorians’ health and move costs on to those least able to pay 
 
 
Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates 
 
Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast 




As an engineer I see the climate problem simply. We have a collection of machines – some burn fossil fuels, others don’t. We need to stop buying the ones that burn poisons and instead buy electric ones and run them on clean electricity. Live well, breathe easy, pay less.
From January, new homes and most new commercial buildings in Victoria will be built all-electric, locking in lower bills and lower emissions. From March, when a gas hot water system dies it must be replaced with an efficient electric one, so existing homes get the savings too. And when a renter’s gas heater fails, the landlord must install efficient electric heating. The tenant’s bills get slashed, not just the owner-occupier’s.

Those laws are now on the ballot because the gas industry has the money and power to unduly influence our politics. Before November’s election, the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation are all promising to scrap them before they start. They say they are defending your “right to choose”.






As One Nation rises, Victoria’s Labor and Liberal parties promise to make abortions free. Is the timing pure politics?

Read more
What they are defending is the right of a few very large, mostly foreign-owned gas companies to keep making enormous profits by making choices for you, choices we know damage your children’s health today and their future tomorrow.
We did the modelling for the Liberals and Nationals under senator Andrew Bragg’s electrification inquiry. One Nation has been harder to reach, though I’ve tried. They could make their own spreadsheets and see the economics is better for electrification.


Three parties are wrapping themselves in the flag and false liberties while opposing the most obviously national-interest energy policy on offer: running as much of Australia as possible on the thing Australia has more of than anyone else. Sunshine.
Here is the moment that matters. Every gas appliance in Victoria will die, on average, once every 15 years or so. The day you replace it is the day the savings are won or lost. Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year


Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate




Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.
The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.

Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.



The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.
The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.
“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”
Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.

articles.raw_rss: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to stop "faffing about" with the North Sea oil and gas fields.

articles.jina_text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said a decision on whether to give the go-ahead to two oil and gas fields will be made "shortly".
Burnham has been deliberating over plans for Rosebank, an oil field off Shetland, and gas field Jackdaw, east of Aberdeen - with a decision on the latter "imminent", according to the energy secretary.
The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.
Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged Burnham "to stop faffing about" when it comes to the North Sea drilling. 
She said: "In July, he said he would approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields in the North Sea. What's he waiting for?
"If he'd approved them back then, we would have British gas warming British homes this winter.
"All of the gas from Jackdaw goes onto the British grid, so will we now stop faffing about and approve Rosebank and Jackdaw?"
















Jackdaw, which is about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.
Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.
The prime minister responded: "She asked me what I'm waiting for – I've had to wait for the government process, which was struck down by the courts under the Conservative government, to be fixed because they messed it up, and we inherited that situation.
"So I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas, we will set out our decisions shortly."
Speaking at the Energy UK Annual Conference, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "We have got all the information on Jackdaw and the department has gone through that so there is a decision that will be imminent".
She added a decision on the development of the Rosebank oil and gas field will take a little longer. 


The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North Sea
Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.










The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.
Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.
They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs. 
Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

A poll for Uswitch suggested that as many as 1.7 million households will turn off their heating to save money on costs, with only 40% planning to turn it on if they get too cold. 








Instead, half of households will turn to hot water bottles, blankets, and extra layers to stay warm. 




It comes as the “Godzilla” El Niño weather phenomenon threatens to bring stormier and colder temperatures to the UK. 




Following the hottest summer on record, temperatures are set to take a tumble as the UK prepares for icy weather and freezing temperatures.

Previous El Niños saw Storm Katie and Storm Desmond wreak havoc across the UK, with record-breaking rainfall and flooding across Lancashire and Cumbria. 




The capital, in particular, was rocked by Storm Katie which bent a construction crane in Greenwich and caused damage to dozens of roofs.

Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences




I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.
In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.



Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins.
As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers.
So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide.

articles.raw_rss: The mission aims to protect the base which is home to the world’s southernmost Post Office.
articles.raw_meta: The mission aims to protect the base which is home to the world’s southernmost Post Office.
articles.jina_text:
A new team of UK specialists is embarking on a 9,000-mile journey to Antarctica to protect a British science base threatened by climate change.
The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust (UKAHT), a Cambridge-based charity, is in its second year of a three-year mission to save Port Lockroy.
Its goal is to restore the site, which has the world's southernmost Post Office, museum, and more than 1,000 gentoo penguins.
This year's team will install beams and props to help the buildings withstand increased precipitation and snow loading, as well as monitor the penguins.
The site is more than 80 years old and faces structural deterioration due to rising temperatures and extreme weather on the rapidly warming Antarctic Peninsula.
After initial assessments revealed serious structural weaknesses, last year's team prepared the site ready for this season's interventions, which UKAHT said was the charity's "biggest ever conservation season" at Port Lockroy.




Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage Trust
Image caption, 

The team will be counting penguin nests, eggs and chicks as part of a study to monitor and protect the colony




Port Lockroy faces escalating deterioration from age, climate change and environmental factors, said UKAHT.
A team of eight will spend five months at remote Base A, Port Lockroy on Goudier Island, while a field team of six specialists will travel further south to carry out the first comprehensive survey of another British heritage site, Wordie House, external, where one of the longest continuous climate records on the continent began.




Image source, UKAHT
Image caption, 

Thousands of cruise ship passengers stop off at the remote Post Office to send messages home




The Port Lockroy team will be led by Carole McCullough, who previously worked in the RAF, and said: "I applied for the role looking for a bit of an adventure, and Antarctica is the ultimate adventure. 
"The teamwork, the bonding, the appreciation of the place - it's all going to make for the most wonderful experience."
She will be joined by others with various life experiences including conservation carpenters and museum and mountain rescue specialists.




Image source, UK Antarctic Heritage Trust
Image caption, 

Postmaster George Clarke, spending his third season at Port Lockroy, said: "I've really fallen in love with the Antarctic wilderness"




Camilla Nichol, UKAHT's chief executive officer, said: "With the demanding conservation season ahead at Port Lockroy and beyond to Wordie House, we have selected a team who bring specialist knowledge and understanding of the Antarctic environment, as well as some much needed enthusiasm and resilience.
"This is a huge year for us as we meet the growing challenges of climate change.
"Since Wordie House's records began in 1947, the Antarctic Peninsula has become one of the fastest-warming places on the planet and we see the impact every year on the wildlife and special places in our care."

US President Donald Trump has also played a role in the debate surrounding the UK's drilling decision.

Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homes 


Hundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung province as shift in wind direction drove blaze towards settlement




A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said on Tuesday as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid.

Read more
“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.
“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”
Another survivor, Haryanti, 50, said strong winds had fuelled the flames, which had torn through homes that were made mostly of wood.
“I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived ... only the clothes on my back,” she said.
Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.

Read more
Indonesia regularly has wildfires during the dry season, but they have been more intense this year because of the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is forecast to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land clearances that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands.
This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.
Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has also grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency.
Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.
The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.

The fire, which burned on peatland, was initially thought to be under control but reignited when wind shifted and drove flames toward the settlement. Survivors reported losing all their belongings, with the disaster compounding Indonesia's wider struggle against devastating wildfires and haze.
